1  ORDER
This Crl.M.C. is filed seeking to quash Annexure-A6 FIR and Annexure-A7 final report in Crime No.1931 of 2016 of Eravipuram Police Station, Kollam.
Now, the case is pending as C.C. No.3514 of 2017 in the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-II, Kollam.

entities.text: Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-II, Kollam
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text: 2. The essential facts of the case are as follows :- The petitioner, who claims to be a 'Paramparya Vaidya' was practising traditional medicine.
He was treating patients at his residence.
The Government of Kerala had issued a Government Order exempting 'Paramparya Vaidyas' from registration.
Later, the said Government Order was set aside by this Court.
On 31.08.2016, the Sub Inspector of Police, Eravipuram Police Station registered a crime against the petitioner alleging offence under Section 420 of IPC.

The Sub Inspector, on obtaining information that the petitioner was treating patients without licence, conducted search in his treatment centre and the police party found that patients were 2025:KER:22205 subjected to treatment there and medicinal oils were used for treatment without any labels in the respective bottles.
The certificates found in the treatment centre, diary kept in the centre, and the medicinal oils were seized and the petitioner was arrested.
3. On conclusion of investigation, final report dated 26.03.2017 produced as Annexure-A7 was filed before the jurisdictional Magistrate's court.
Allegations in the FIR are repeated in the final report also.
The offence under Section 420 of IPC is the only offence alleged against the petitioner in the final report.
4. The learned counsel for the petitioner submitted that the petitioner had not committed any offence as alleged by the police.
He argued that even if the entire allegations in the final report are accepted as correct, the same are not sufficient to constitute the ingredients of the offence under Section 420 of IPC.

The police recorded statements of some persons, who had availed treatments from the petitioner's centre, but none of them had given any statements sufficient to constitute the ingredients of the alleged offence.

He pointed out that a reading of the statements of the persons who had underwent treatment would show that the police officers told them that the petitioner was not an authorised medical practitioner to treat the patients.
He has further stated that only 2025:KER:22205 thereafter they gave statements that the petitioner was not an authorised medical practitioner.

Learned counsel further submitted that at the relevant time, the Government Order granting exemption to the 'Paramparya Vaidyas' was in force and therefore, there was nothing illegal in practising as a 'Paramparya Vaidya'.
He also submitted that even the want of registration will not make out any offence under the Indian Penal Code though provisions of other statute may be attracted.
5. I have heard learned Public Prosecutor also.
The learned Public Prosecutor supported the police case and submitted that the petitioner has to face trial as serious allegations have been raised in the final report.

6. On hearing the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor and on a perusal of the records, I am of the view that the ingredients to attract the offence under Section 420 Udayabhanu vs State Of Kerala on 12 March, 2025 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/40918973/
2 of IPC are not made out in the final report.
The registration of the case by the police was for the reason that the petitioner was not a qualified medical practitioner and had no licence to treat the patients.

As rightly submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner, at the relevant point of time,
the Government had granted exemption to the 'Paramparya Vaidyas' for practising.

Even otherwise,
practising medicine without licence cannot be 2025:KER:22205 considered as an offence under Section 420 of IPC unless the well established ingredients of the offence are attracted in the facts and circumstances of the case.
Here, in the case at hand, none has given any statement to the police that they were cheated in the sense of the word as used in the IPC.

Even if the petitioner was found practising without proper authorisation or licence, it may attract the provisions of other relevant laws and not attract the offence under Section 420 of IPC as alleged by the prosecution.
Therefore, I find that the prosecution proceeded on the basis of the impugned FIR and the final report amounts to abuse of process of law.
Hence, the Crl.M.C. is allowed.

The FIR and the final report in Crime No.1931 of 2016 of Eravipuram Police Station, Kollam and the proceedings in C.C. No.3514 of 2017 pending before the Judicial First Class Magistrate Court-II, Kollam are hereby quashed.
